input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Discuss implications for audit-friendly workflows and reproducible science given JSON-constrained section outputs and LaTeX/bib integration. Propose future extensions that enhance auditability (automated citation-assertion checks, provenance tracking), reproducibility (releaseable pipelines, config schemas), and evaluation (broader topical coverage, human reviewer studies).

output:
The following discussion is presented as general background knowledge: no external evidence excerpts were provided to support specific empirical claims in this section, and the statements below should be interpreted as design recommendations and hypotheses rather than verified results.

We argue that machine-readable section outputs and straightforward LaTeX/refs.bib assembly create practical affordances for auditability and reproducibility. In particular, enforcing a strict JSON schema per section (containing explicit fields for the rendered text, a list of cited evidence identifiers, and provenance metadata) can produce a compact, verifiable record for each authored unit. Such records facilitate automated checks (schema conformance, presence of required citation entries) and simplify human inspection by collating the text alongside its asserted sources. (General background knowledge.)

We propose several concrete extensions to improve auditability and to support reproducible pipelines. Each proposal is stated as a recommended direction rather than an empirically validated improvement.

- Automated citation–assertion checking. Require generated sections to attach evidence identifiers to discrete factual claims (for example, by associating each sentence or claim span with one or more evidence_ids). Downstream tools can then verify that every claim marked as factual has at least one associated evidence item and flag claims lacking provenance for human review. (General background knowledge.)

- Fine-grained provenance tracking. Record, for each injected evidence snippet, the source document identifier, retrieval query, retrieval score/rank, snippet character offsets, and any transformation applied (e.g., truncation or normalization). Storing this provenance alongside the section JSON enables reproducible re-retrieval and supports targeted audits that trace an unsupported claim back to its retrieval context. (General background knowledge.)

- Releaseable pipelines and configuration schemas. Package the end-to-end workflow (retrieval components, prompt templates, JSON schema definitions, and assembly scripts) with explicit versioning of software dependencies and model checkpoints. Provide canonical configuration files (e.g., YAML or JSON) that specify retrieval index snapshots, prompt template versions, and schema versions so that manuscript generation can be re-run deterministically where possible. (General background knowledge.)

- Evaluation extensions. Broaden evaluation along two axes: topical breadth (additional domains and document types) and human-centered assessment (structured reviewer studies that rate citation fidelity, perceived support for claims, and ease of audit). Define reproducible evaluation protocols that operate over the JSON outputs (for example, measuring fraction of factual claims with attached evidence_ids) to enable automated comparisons across systems. (General background knowledge.)

We also note practical limitations and risks that any audit-oriented workflow must address: dependence on retrieval quality (poor candidate evidence reduces the utility of provenance records), the potential for schema rigidness to impede iterative writing workflows, and the need to balance automated blocking checks with human-in-the-loop remediation to avoid excessive false positives. Each of these points motivates future empirical study and careful operational design. (General background knowledge.)

In summary, adopting JSON-constrained section outputs and explicit provenance fields can make long-form generation workflows more audit-friendly and reproducible in principle. Realizing these benefits in practice requires implementation of automated citation–assertion checks, comprehensive provenance capture, well-versioned pipeline releases, and thorough evaluation across domains; we present these items as a concrete agenda for future work. (General background knowledge.)
